'''Sheepshead Bay''' is a neighborhood in southern [[Brooklyn]], [[New York City]]. It is bounded by [[Ocean Parkway (Brooklyn)|Ocean Parkway]] to the west; [[Kings Highway (Brooklyn)|Kings Highway]] to the north; [[Nostrand Avenue]] and Gerritsen Avenue to the east; and the [[Atlantic Ocean]] to the south. Sheepshead Bay is abutted by the neighborhoods of [[Brighton Beach]], [[Manhattan Beach, Brooklyn|Manhattan Beach]], [[Coney Island]] and [[Homecrest, Brooklyn|Homecrest]], to the west; [[Midwood]] to the north; and [[Gerritsen Beach]] to the east.

The neighborhood is named after a bay that separates mainland Brooklyn from the eastern portion of [[Coney Island]] & the Southern portion of [[Manhattan Beach, Brooklyn|Manhattan Beach]] & [[Brighton Beach]] which was originally one of the [[Outer Barrier]] islands but is now a peninsula. The mouth of the bay is about {{convert|1.0|mi|km}} southwest of [[Marine Park]].

Sheepshead Bay is part of [[Brooklyn Community Board 15|Brooklyn Community District 15]], and its primary [[ZIP Code]]s are 11229 and 11235.<ref name="NYCPlanning"/> It is patrolled by the 61st Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department]].<ref name="NYPD 61st Precinct"/> Politically it is represented by the [[New York City Council]]'s 46th and 48th Districts.

==History==

=== Fishing and tourism destination ===
[[File:Races, Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn, ca. 1872-1887. (5832932151).jpg|thumb|left|Races, c. 1872–1887]]
The name "Sheepshead Bay" applies to the neighborhood north of the bay as well as the bay itself. Sheepshead Bay was named for the [[Sheepshead (Archosargus)|sheepshead]], an edible fish found in the bay's waters.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Naming of Sheepshead Bay |last=Davis |first=Nicole |website=Brooklyn Based |date=July 12, 2013 |url= https://brooklynbased.com/2009/05/19/the-naming-of-sheepshead-bay/}}</ref><ref name="Stiles 1884">{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/cu31924088998046|title=The Civil, Political, Professional and Ecclesiastical History, and Commercial and Industrial Record of the County of Kings and the City of Brooklyn, N. Y. from 1683 to 1884|last1=Stiles|first1=H.R.|last2=Brockett|first2=L.P.|last3=Proctor|first3=L.B.|publisher=Munsell|year=1884|series=New York: county and regional histories and atlases|page=[https://archive.org/details/cu31924088998046/page/172 172]|access-date=July 26, 2019}}</ref>{{Rp|183}} Originally an extension of the [[Gravesend, Brooklyn|town of Gravesend]] to the west, Sheepshead Bay was a secluded fishing and farming community early in its history.<ref name="Stiles 1884" />{{Rp|184}}<ref name="NYCL-0972" />{{Rp|2}}

Starting in the 1840s, residents of Brooklyn and Manhattan were drawn to the community as a summer destination. Hunters and fishermen started coming to Sheepshead Bay and various restaurants and hotels were erected.<ref name="Stiles 1884" />{{Rp|184}}<ref name="NYCL-0972">{{cite web|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/1706.pdf |title=F.W.I.W. Lundy Brothers Restaurant Building|date=March 3, 1992|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=July 28, 2019}}</ref>{{Rp|2}} Sheepshead Bay's allure as a fishing destination was further helped by the opening of [[Ocean Avenue (Brooklyn)|Ocean Avenue]] in 1876 and the extension of the [[Long Island Rail Road]]'s [[Manhattan Beach Branch]] in 1877–1878, which brought visitors both to the community of Sheepshead Bay and to the [[Manhattan Beach, Brooklyn|Manhattan Beach]] resort across the bay. The first of the community's farms was split up into several lots for residential development in 1877.<ref name="NYCL-0972" />{{Rp|2}}<ref>{{cite book|title=Gravesend, the home of Coney Island|last=Ierardi|first=Eric|publisher=Arcadia|year=2001|isbn=978-0-7385-2361-3|location=Charleston, S.C|oclc=51632931}}</ref> Three years later the [[Sheepshead Bay Race Track]] opened in the neighborhood,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1879/09/03/archives/coney-island-jockey-club-programme-for-the-september-meeting-a.html|title=CONEY ISLAND JOCKEY CLUB.; PROGRAMME FOR THE SEPTEMBER MEETING-- A PROMISE OF GOOD SPORT.|date=September 28, 2018|website=The New York Times|access-date=September 7, 2019}}</ref> bringing even more visitors during the spring and fall. Near the racecourse, racing investor [[William Collins Whitney]] constructed a training track.<ref name="NYCL-0972" />{{Rp|2}} A "Millionaire's Row" was built on Emmons Avenue east of East 27th Street,<ref name="The Weekly Nabe 2012">{{cite web|url=http://theweeklynabe.com/2012/08/27/sheepshead-bay-brooklyn-history/|title=Sheepshead Bay: built on the bay of Kings|date=August 27, 2012|website=The Weekly Nabe|access-date=September 7, 2019|archive-date=May 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190530144528/http://theweeklynabe.com/2012/08/27/sheepshead-bay-brooklyn-history/|url-status=dead}}</ref> while socialites tended to go to restaurants such as Tappan's.<ref name="NYCL-0972" />{{Rp|2}}

The track would continue to operate as a horse-racing course until 1910 when horse betting was criminalized in New York state.<ref name="NYCL-0972" />{{Rp|2}}<ref>{{cite web|url=https://drf.uky.edu/catalog/1910s/drf1910052701/drf1910052701_1_3|title=Anti-Racing Bills Pass at Albany|date=May 27, 1910|publisher=Daily Racing Form at University of Kentucky Archives|access-date=November 30, 2018}}</ref> Afterward it operated as an auto racing track from 1915 to 1919.<ref name="NYCL-0972" />{{Rp|2}}<ref>{{cite web|url=https://drf.uky.edu/catalog/1910s/drf1919120401/drf1919120401_1_7|title=Last of Famous Sheepshead Bay: Former Home of the Suburban Handicap and Futurity Cut Up into Building Lots|date=December 4, 1919|publisher=Daily Racing Form at University of Kentucky Archives|access-date=November 30, 2018}}</ref> The decline of the Sheepshead Bay Race Track, along with the construction of amusement parks at nearby [[Coney Island]] and the proximity of Coney Island's attractions to the newly built [[New York City Subway|subway]], led to the decline of Sheepshead Bay as a tourist destination.<ref name="The Weekly Nabe 2012" /> Passenger rail service on the Manhattan Beach Branch ceased in 1924,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://brooklyneagle.com/articles/2012/09/09/when-brooklyn-had-its-own-railroad-lines/|title=When Brooklyn had its own railroad lines|date=September 9, 2012|website=Brooklyn Eagle|language=en-US|access-date=September 8, 2019}}</ref> and the line was formally abandoned in 1937.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1937/05/18/archives/long-island-r-r-files-plea.html|title=Long Island R. R. Files Plea|date=May 18, 1937|newspaper=The New York Times|access-date=September 17, 2017|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The former race track site was subdivided for the construction of housing, and Millionaire's Row was soon lined with bungalows.<ref name="The Weekly Nabe 2012" /> The closure of the race track resulted in a plethora of newly vacant plots in the community of Sheepshead Bay, and by extension, an influx of residents.<ref name="NYCL-0972" />{{Rp|2}}

=== Filling of creek and waterfront development ===
[[File:Sheepshead Bay.jpg|thumb|Sheepshead Bay, facing east|alt=|left]]
The bay itself was originally the easterly entrance to [[Coney Island Creek]], which was {{Convert|3|mi||abbr=}} long and minimally navigable through the 20th century.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://hiddenwatersblog.wordpress.com/2016/01/12/canal-avenue-brooklyn/|title=Canal Avenue, Brooklyn|first=Sergey|last=Kadinsky|date=January 12, 2016}}</ref> A map from 1898 shows that numerous inlets protruded from the bay into the community.<ref name="The Weekly Nabe 2012" /> From the late 19th century through the early 20th century there were plans to turn the creek into the ''Gravesend Ship Canal''.<ref>[http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/B379/ NYC Parks Dept] Coney Island Creek Park</ref> The plan including re-dredging the creek into a canal running in a straight east–west line and filling all the marsh land either side of the creek to expand the urban [[Grid plan|grid]] to the edge of the canal. However, this never happened.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://hiddenwatersblog.wordpress.com/2016/01/12/canal-avenue-brooklyn/|title=Canal Avenue, Brooklyn|last=Kadinsky|first=Sergey|date=January 12, 2016|website=Hidden Waters blog|language=en|access-date=September 8, 2019}}</ref> Squan Creek, a tributary of the Coney Island Creek, ran through the Sheepshead Bay neighborhood. While Squan Creek was infilled in the 1920s, its route is still evidenced by Sheepshead Bay Road's crooked route through the street grid, as well as the presence of several dead-end streets that used to abut the creek's route.<ref>{{Cite Hidden Waters NYC}}</ref>

With the development of the Sheepshead Bay community into a residential neighborhood, there were efforts to improve the facilities on the waterfront. The channel of the Sheepshead Bay waterway was [[Dredging|dredged]] by 1916 to allow fishing boats to dock there; previously these craft had to dock at [[Canarsie, Brooklyn|Canarsie]].<ref name="NYCL-0972" />{{Rp|2}} In 1922 the [[New York City Dock Commission]] proposed to dredge the bays further, build [[Bulkhead (barrier)|bulkheads]] on the shore, and widen Emmons Avenue on the waterfront from {{Convert|80|to|120|ft|abbr=}}.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/35726717/|title=Delaney Urges City to Spend $1,000,000 at Sheepshead Bay|date=October 18, 1922|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=September 8, 2019|page=2|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}}}</ref> 25 piers would be built on the south side of Emmons Avenue while 26 buildings, including a new [[Lundy's Restaurant]] location, would be built on the north side.<ref name="NYCL-0972" />{{Rp|2}} Residents expressed concerns that the bay might become a commercial shipping port, and local fishermen opposed the city's plan to establish a fish market there.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/35727368/|title=Fish Market Plan Opposed by Civics|date=August 4, 1932|work=Brooklyn Times-Union|access-date=September 7, 2019|page=7|via=newspapers.com {{open access}}}}</ref> A compromise to use Sheepshead Bay only for private and charter boats was reached in 1929,<ref name="NYCL-0972" />{{Rp|2}} and the city built several piers at an angle from the bulkhead to prevent trucks from loading onto these piers.<ref name="The Weekly Nabe 2012" />

In 1931, the city condemned several buildings on the bay shore, including the original Lundy's Restaurant, to widen Emmons Avenue.<ref name="The Weekly Nabe 2012" /> The [[Great Depression]] delayed further progress, as these buildings would not be destroyed until mid-1934, and construction started on new buildings on Emmons Avenue's northern sidewalk.<ref name="NYCL-0972" />{{Rp|3}} At that point a newspaper article noted that Emmons Avenue had been "transformed by attractive looking restaurants and stores."<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/35728331/|title=New Buildings Transforming Sheepshead Bay|date=June 3, 1934|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=September 8, 2019|page=41|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}}}</ref> In 1936, the city and the owners of the condemned buildings reached a monetary [[Settlement (litigation)|settlement]],<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/35728088/|title=Court Ruling Speeds Sheepshead Waterfront Changes|date=March 8, 1936|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=September 8, 2019|page=60|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}}}</ref> and by the following year, the channel had been dredged and ten docks had been constructed.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bklyn.newspapers.com/clip/35729094/|title=Sheepshead Bay in Modern Dress after Federal Project|date=August 21, 1937|work=Brooklyn Daily Eagle|access-date=September 8, 2019|page=13|via=Brooklyn Public Library; newspapers.com {{open access}}}}</ref> The filling-in of the central part of the Coney Island during the 1930s, in conjunction with construction of the Shore Parkway portion of the [[Belt Parkway]].<ref name="NYTimes-GhostShips-2006">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/08/06/nyregion/thecity/06grav.html/partner/rssnyt|title=The Ghost Ships of Coney Island Creek|author=Lamb|first=Jonah Owen|date=August 6, 2006|work=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=June 11, 2014}}</ref> Shore Parkway opened in 1941, and soon afterward, the last remaining farms in Sheepshead Bay were redeveloped into residential buildings.<ref name="The Weekly Nabe 2012" />

=== Later development ===
Sheepshead Bay became populated by Jewish and Soviet immigrants during the late 20th century, similar to neighboring Brighton Beach.<ref name="The Weekly Nabe 2012" /> In 1978, in one of the largest disasters in Sheepshead Bay's modern history, six firefighters were killed while fighting the [[Waldbaum's supermarket fire]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/ny-metro-walbaums-forty-years-20180801-story.html|title=Unified in tragedy: Families of fallen firefighters grow together 40 years after Waldbaum's blaze|last=Tracy|first=Thomas|website=nydailynews.com|date=August 2, 2018 |access-date=September 8, 2019}}</ref> Sheepshead Bay did not undergo the [[white flight]] and high crime that afflicted other New York City neighborhoods. Lundy's closed in 1979, resulting in the closure of retail on Emmons Avenue.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1979/11/05/archives/brooklyn-area-counts-on-lundys-heirs-the-talk-of-sheepshead-bay.html|title=Brooklyn Area Counts on Lundy's Heirs|date=November 5, 1979|website=The New York Times|access-date=September 8, 2019}}</ref> After the closure of Lundy's, Sheepshead Bay transformed from a predominantly Irish and Italian enclave into a more racially diverse neighborhood, and the population became increasingly elderly. Recreational fishing along the bay also started to decline in the surrounding community.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1991/07/08/nyregion/sheepshead-bay-losing-its-old-salt-air.html|title=Sheepshead Bay Losing Its Old-Salt Air|date=July 8, 1991|website=The New York Times|access-date=September 10, 2019}}</ref> In the 1970s, the city created a maritime [[zoning]] district on Emmons Avenue to promote waterfront development.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424053111904106704576582941385699126|title=Division in Sheepshead Bay|last=Barbanel|first=Josh|date=September 21, 2011|website=WSJ|access-date=September 10, 2019}}</ref> The [[Roll-A-Palace|Sheepshead Bay Roll-A-Palace]], a [[roller disco]] rink that opened in the neighborhood in 1977,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lawrence |first=Peter D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=99GnsmH6yhkC&q=%22roll-a-palace%22 |title=A Kids' New York |date=1982 |publisher=Avon |isbn=978-0-380-81315-5 |language=en}}</ref> welcomed over 5,000 customers per weekend at its peak.<ref name="google">{{Cite magazine |date=1979 |title=What's Hot? What's Not? |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ogkwAQAAIAAJ&q=%22you+will+find+the+front+-+runner+of+the+roller%22 |magazine=Cue: The Weekly Magazine of New York Life |publisher=Cue Publishing Company |language=en |quote=... the front - runner of the roller - disco craze , a fabulous $ 2 million roller disco in a former movie theater that has been earning its $ 4 ( including skates ) admission price for the past two years . Spic and span , it looks for all ...}}</ref><ref name="google2">{{Cite magazine |last=Riedinger |first=Bob Jr. |date=1979-03-03 |title=Going Back to the 1870s: Skating To Music |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=KyUEAAAAMBAJ&dq=%22roll-a-palace%22&pg=PT56 |magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |pages=48, 57 |language=en}}</ref>

In the last decade of the 20th century, a real estate boom brought the reopening of Lundy's Restaurant,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/03/17/nyregion/neighborhood-report-manhattan-beachsheepshead-baylundys-leads-a.html|title=NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: MANHATTAN BEACH/SHEEPSHEAD BAY;Lundy's Leads a Street's Revival|date=March 17, 1996|website=The New York Times|access-date=September 8, 2019}}</ref> which was made a city landmark in 1992.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://s-media.nyc.gov/agencies/lpc/lp/0972.pdf|title=F.W.I.W. Lundy Brothers Restaurant Building|date=March 3, 1992|publisher=[[New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission]]|access-date=July 28, 2019}}</ref> Furthermore, [[Loehmann's]] proposed a store in Sheepshead Bay in 1993, the first major development in the area in several years,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/07/19/nyregion/strictly-business-sheepshead-bay-at-odds-on-a-waterfront-proposal.html|title=STRICTLY BUSINESS; Sheepshead Bay at Odds on a Waterfront Proposal|date=July 19, 1993|website=The New York Times|access-date=September 10, 2019}}</ref> though the city rejected initial plans for the development after community opposition.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/01/23/nyregion/neighborhood-report-sheepshead-bay-with-regret-city-rejects-loehmann-s.html|title=NEIGHBORHOOD REPORT: SHEEPSHEAD BAY; With Regret, City Rejects Loehmann's|date=January 23, 1994|website=The New York Times|access-date=September 10, 2019}}</ref> After another proposal for a Loehmann's shopping center was rejected, Mayor [[Rudy Giuliani]]'s administration approved a smaller version of the shopping center in the late 1990s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/brooklyn/loehmann-plan-reignites-20-year-battle-sheepshead-bay-article-1.1954448|title=Loehmann's plan reignites 20-year battle in Sheepshead Bay|last=Blau|first=Reuven|date=September 29, 2014|website=nydailynews.com|access-date=September 10, 2019}}</ref> Meanwhile, the reopening of Lundy's in 1995 spurred a wave of development on Emmons Avenue. By March 1996, property owners reported that real estate prices had doubled and that vacant apartments were being occupied.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1996/03/17/nyregion/neighborhood-report-manhattan-beachsheepshead-baylundys-leads-a.html|title=Neighborhood Report: Manhattan Beach/Sheepshead Bay; Lundy's Leads a Street's Revival|date=March 17, 1996|website=The New York Times|access-date=September 8, 2019}}</ref> With new development, housing prices in the area increased sharply, and there were concerns about a dearth of parking, since the new developments had collectively resulted in the removal of 2,000 parking spots in Sheepshead Bay.<ref name="The New York Times 2003">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2003/03/30/realestate/if-you-re-thinking-living-sheepshead-bay-brooklyn-where-water-big-part-community.html|title=If You're Thinking of Living In/Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn; Where Water Is Big Part of Community|date=March 30, 2003|website=The New York Times|access-date=September 10, 2019}}</ref> Also in the mid-1990s, a small amusement park called Fun Time USA opened on Knapp Street, operating for almost 11 years before closing in 2005.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/10/16/nyregion/the-partys-over.html|title=The Party's Over|last=Mooney|first=Jake|date=October 16, 2005|work=The New York Times|access-date=January 7, 2020|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

Lundy's closed again in 2007;<ref name="offthemenu">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/02/14/dining/14off.html|title=Off the Menu|last=Fabricant|first=Florence|date=February 14, 2007|website=The New York Times|access-date=September 9, 2019}}</ref> a shopping center took its place.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/09/30/nyregion/30lundys.html|title=Renovation of Lundy's Stirs Dispute in Brooklyn|last=Fahim|first=Kareem|date=September 30, 2008|website=The New York Times|access-date=September 9, 2019}}</ref> Soviet-style restaurants/nightclubs opened along the waterfront.<ref name="The New York Times 2003" /> Sheepshead Bay has also experienced a growth of condominium developments,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/09/18/realestate/transformation-on-brooklyns-southern-shore.html|title=Transformation on Brooklyn's Southern Shore|date=September 18, 2016|website=The New York Times|access-date=September 10, 2019}}</ref> and on Emmons Avenue, the northern shoreline street along the bay, are piers boasting an active seafood market and tour boats.<ref name="The New York Times 2003" />

== Land use ==
Sheepshead Bay is mostly residential. Low-density, one- and two-family attached and semi-attached houses are common near the western and eastern edges of the neighborhood. Higher-density [[condominium]]s and [[housing cooperative|co-ops]] are more common near Ocean Avenue, at the center of the neighborhood.<ref name="Mooney 2011">{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/05/22/realestate/calm-and-clamor-in-equal-measure-living-insheepshead-bay-brooklyn.html|title=Calm and Clamor, in Equal Measure – Living In/Sheepshead Bay, Brooklyn|last=Mooney|first=Jake|date=May 20, 2011|website=The New York Times|access-date=September 10, 2019}}</ref> Housing developments include [[Sheepshead Bay-Nostrand Houses]] managed by [[New York City Housing Authority|NYCHA]] and two [[Mitchell-Lama Housing Program]] co-ops.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Mitchell-Lama Housing Companies and Redevelopment Companies | url=https://www.nyc.gov/assets/hpd/downloads/pdfs/services/MLLIST.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200101234159/https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/hpd/downloads/pdfs/services/MLLIST.pdf | archive-date=2020-01-01}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web | title=ArcGIS Web Application | url=https://nycha.maps.arcgis.com/apps/webappviewer/index.html?id=41c6ff5e73ec459092e982060b7cf1a1 | access-date=2026-07-18 | website=nycha.maps.arcgis.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| title=Sheepshead Bay | url=https://www.nyc.gov/assets/nycha/downloads/pdf/Sheepshead%20Bay.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151010055651/http://www1.nyc.gov:80/assets/nycha/downloads/pdf/Sheepshead%20Bay.pdf | archive-date=2015-10-10}}</ref>

==Demographics==
[[File:Poole Lane last bungalo jeh.JPG|thumb|Many homes like this were built in the 1920s|alt=]]
Based on data from the [[2010 United States census]], the population of Sheepshead Bay was 64,518, a change of −78 (−0.1%) from the 64,596 counted in [[2000 United States census|2000]]. The entirety of Community Board 15, which comprises Sheepshead Bay, had 173,961 inhabitants as of [[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene|NYC Health]]'s 2018 Community Health Profile, with an average life expectancy of 83.7 years.<ref name="CHP2018">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/data/2018chp-bk15.pdf|title=Sheepshead Bay (Including Gerritsen Beach, Gravesend, Homecrest, Kings Highway, Manhattan Beach, Plumb Beach and Sheepshead Bay)|date=2018|website=nyc.gov|publisher=NYC Health|access-date=March 2, 2019}}</ref>{{Rp|2, 20}} This is higher than the median life expectancy of 81.2 for all New York City neighborhoods.<ref name="nyc.gov 2016">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/tcny/community-health-assessment-plan.pdf|title=2016–2018 Community Health Assessment and Community Health Improvement Plan: Take Care New York 2020|date=2016|website=[[government of New York City|nyc.gov]]|publisher=[[New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene]]|access-date=September 8, 2017}}</ref>{{Rp|53 (PDF p. 84)}}<ref>{{cite web | title=New Yorkers are living longer, happier and healthier lives | website=New York Post | last=Short | first=Aaron | date=June 4, 2017 | url=https://nypost.com/2017/06/04/new-yorkers-are-living-longer-happier-and-healthier-lives/ | access-date=March 1, 2019}}</ref> Most inhabitants are middle-aged adults and youth: 21% are between the ages of 0–17, 28% between 25 and 44, and 26% between 45 and 64. The ratio of college-aged and elderly residents was lower, at 8% and 17% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|2}}

As of 2016, the median [[household income]] in Community Board 15 was $61,274.<ref name="CB15PUMA">{{cite news|url=https://censusreporter.org/profiles/79500US3604016-nyc-brooklyn-community-district-15-sheepshead-bay-gerritsen-beach-homecrest-puma-ny/|title=NYC-Brooklyn Community District 15—Sheepshead Bay, Gerritsen Beach & Homecrest PUMA, NY|newspaper=Census Reporter|access-date=July 17, 2018}}</ref> In 2018, an estimated 19% of Sheepshead Bay residents lived in poverty, compared to 21% in all of Brooklyn and 20% in all of New York City. One in twelve residents (8%) were unemployed, compared to 9% in the rest of both Brooklyn and New York City. Rent burden, or the percentage of residents who have difficulty paying their rent, is 53% in Sheepshead Bay, slightly higher than the citywide and boroughwide rates of 52% and 51% respectively. Based on this calculation, {{as of|2018|lc=y}}, Sheepshead Bay is considered to be high-income relative to the rest of the city and not [[gentrification|gentrifying]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|7}}

In the 2020 census data from [[New York City Department of City Planning]], southern Sheepshead Bay and nearby [[Manhattan Beach, Brooklyn|Manhattan Beach]]/[[Gerritsen Beach, Brooklyn|Gerritsen Beach]] is still an overwhelming majority White population of 40,000 or more residents, between 10,000 and 19,999 Asian residents, and between 5,000 and 9,999 Hispanic residents. Meanwhile, the northern section called Madison has between 20,000 and 29,999 White residents and 5,000 to 9,999 Asian residents, while the Black and Hispanic populations were less than 5000 residents each. ==Police and crime==
Sheepshead Bay is patrolled by the 61st Precinct of the [[New York City Police Department|NYPD]], located at 2575 Coney Island Avenue.<ref name="NYPD 61st Precinct">{{Cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/nypd/bureaus/patrol/precincts/61st-precinct.page|title=NYPD – 61st Precinct|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=October 3, 2016}}</ref>
The 61st Precinct ranked 5th safest out of 69 patrol areas for per-capita crime in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/brooklyn/sheepshead-bay/|title=Sheepshead Bay – DNAinfo.com Crime and Safety Report|website=www.dnainfo.com|access-date=October 6, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170415051938/https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/crime-safety-report/brooklyn/sheepshead-bay|archive-date=April 15, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> {{As of|2018}}, with a non-fatal assault rate of 22 per 100,000 people, Sheepshead Bay's rate of [[violent crime]]s per capita is less than that of the city as a whole. The incarceration rate of 200 per 100,000 people is lower than that of the city as a whole.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|8}}

The 61st Precinct has a lower crime rate than in the 1990s, with crimes across all categories having decreased by 88.2% between 1990 and 2018. The precinct reported one murder, 17 rapes, 150 robberies, 170 felony assaults, 169 burglaries, 584 grand larcenies, and 72 grand larcenies auto in 2018.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/nypd/downloads/pdf/crime_statistics/cs-en-us-061pct.pdf|title=61st Precinct CompStat Report|website=www.nyc.gov|publisher=[[New York City Police Department]]|access-date=July 22, 2018}}</ref>

== Health ==
{{As of|2018}}, [[preterm birth]]s and births to teenage mothers are less common in Sheepshead Bay than in other places citywide. In Sheepshead Bay, there were 66 preterm births per 1,000 live births (compared to 87 per 1,000 citywide), and 12.4 births to teenage mothers per 1,000 live births (compared to 19.3 per 1,000 citywide).<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|11}} Sheepshead Bay has a relatively high population of residents who are [[Health insurance coverage in the United States|uninsured]], or who receive healthcare through [[Medicaid]].<ref name="New York City Health Provider Partnership Brooklyn Community Needs Assessment">[http://www.health.ny.gov/health_care/medicaid/redesign/dsrip/pps_applications/docs/maimonides_medical_center/3.8_maimonides_cna.pdf New York City Health Provider Partnership Brooklyn Community Needs Assessment: Final Report], [[New York Academy of Medicine]] (October 3, 2014).</ref> In 2018, this population of uninsured residents was estimated to be 4%, which is lower than the citywide rate of 12%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|14}}

The concentration of [[particulates|fine particulate matter]], the deadliest type of [[air pollution|air pollutant]], in Sheepshead Bay is {{convert|0.0068|mg/m3|oz/ft3}}, lower than the citywide and boroughwide averages.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|9}} Seventeen percent of Sheepshead Bay residents are [[Smoking|smokers]], which is slightly higher than the city average of 14% of residents being smokers.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} In Sheepshead Bay, 26% of residents are [[Obesity|obese]], 9% are [[Diabetes mellitus|diabetic]], and 25% have [[hypertension|high blood pressure]]—compared to the citywide averages of 24%, 11%, and 28% respectively.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|16}} In addition, 17% of children are obese, compared to the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|12}}

Ninety-three percent of residents eat some fruits and vegetables every day, which is higher than the city's average of 87%. In 2018, 70% of residents described their health as "good", "very good", or "excellent", less than the city's average of 78%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|13}} For every supermarket in Sheepshead Bay, there are 25 [[convenience store|bodegas]].<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|10}}

The nearest large hospital is the [[Coney Island Hospital]].<ref name="New York City Health Provider Partnership Brooklyn Community Needs Assessment"/>

== Education ==
Sheepshead Bay generally has a higher ratio of college-educated residents than the rest of the city {{as of|2018|lc=y}}. A plurality of residents (47%) have a college education or higher, while 15% have less than a high school education and 38% are high school graduates or have some college education. By contrast, 40% of Brooklynites and 38% of city residents have a college education or higher.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} The percentage of Sheepshead Bay students excelling in math rose from 49 percent in 2000 to 66 percent in 2011, but reading achievement dropped from 54% to 52% during the same time period.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://furmancenter.org/files/sotc/BK_15_11.pdf|title=Sheepshead Bay – BK 15|date=2011|publisher=[[Furman Center for Real Estate and Urban Policy]]|access-date=October 5, 2016}}</ref>

Sheepshead Bay's rate of elementary school student absenteeism is about equal to the rest of New York City. In Sheepshead Bay, 16% of elementary school students missed twenty or more days per [[school year]], less than the citywide average of 20%.<ref name="nyc.gov 2016" />{{Rp|24 (PDF p. 55)}}<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}} Additionally, 82% of high school students in Sheepshead Bay graduate on time, more than the citywide average of 75%.<ref name="CHP2018" />{{Rp|6}}

===Schools===
Several public schools serve the community: [[James Madison High School (New York)|James Madison High School]]; Abraham Lincoln High School, JHS 14 Shell Bank Intermediate School; [[The Bay Academy]]; and elementary schools P.S.194 PS 254, PS 206, PS 209, PS 225 and PS 52. Private schools in the area include St. Mark Catholic Academy, St. Edmund's School, and the [[Brooklyn Amity School]]. [[Kingsborough Community College]] of the [[City University of New York]] (CUNY) is nearby. The former [[Sheepshead Bay High School]] closed in 2016.

=== Libraries ===
The [[Brooklyn Public Library]] has four branches in Sheepshead Bay.

The Sheepshead Bay branch is located at 2636 East 14th Street, near Avenue Z. The branch has occupied four buildings since it was founded in 1903. The current {{convert|7475|ft2|m2|adj=on}} building opened in 1963.<ref>{{cite web | title=Sheepshead Bay Library | website=Brooklyn Public Library | date=August 22, 2011 | url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/sheepshead-bay | access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref>

The Kings Bay branch is located at 3650 Nostrand Avenue between Avenues W and X. It opened in 1951, and has occupied its current location since 1959.<ref>{{cite web | title=Kings Bay Library | website=Brooklyn Public Library | date=August 19, 2011 | url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/kings-bay | access-date=February 21, 2019}}</ref>

The Kings Highway branch is located at 2115 Ocean Ave, just south of the Midwood neighborhood. Originally opened in 1910 as an unstaffed deposit station, it moved several times during the early 20th century before arriving at its current location in 1954. The current building was the first branch library built in Brooklyn by the City of New York. The branch also includes a US Passport Office.<ref>{{cite web | title=Kings Highway Library | website=Brooklyn Public Library | date=August 22, 2011 | url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/kings-highway | access-date=February 19, 2022}}</ref>

The Homecrest branch is located at 2525 Coney Island Ave, just south of Avenue V.<ref>{{cite web | title=Homecrest Library | website=Brooklyn Public Library | date=August 19, 2011 | url=https://www.bklynlibrary.org/locations/homecrest | access-date=February 19, 2022}}</ref>

==Transportation==
===Public transportation===
[[New York City Subway]] service to Sheepshead Bay is provided by the [[BMT Brighton Line]] ({{NYCS trains|Brighton}}), with local stops at [[Avenue U (BMT Brighton Line)|Avenue U]] and [[Neck Road (BMT Brighton Line)|Neck Road]], and express/local stops at the [[Kings Highway (BMT Brighton Line)|Kings Highway]] and [[Sheepshead Bay (BMT Brighton Line)|Sheepshead Bay]] stations.

[[New York City Bus]] routes in the area include the {{NYC bus link|B3|B4|B36|B44|B44 SBS|B49|B68|prose=y}} local buses and the {{NYC bus link|BM3}} express bus. The Madison subsection is also served by the {{NYC bus link|B2|B7|B31|B82|B82 SBS|B100|BM4|prose=y}}.<ref>{{cite NYC bus map|B}}</ref>

===Main thoroughfares===
The main shopping and business thoroughfares are Emmons Avenue, Sheepshead Bay Road, [[Avenue U]], [[Ocean Avenue (Brooklyn)|Ocean Avenue]], and [[Nostrand Avenue]]. Emmons Avenue is at the west end of the [[Belt Parkway#Shore Parkway|Shore Greenway]] which lies between Shore Parkway and Jamaica Bay, connecting eastward and northward to [[Canarsie]] and [[Cross Bay Boulevard]]. Emmons Avenue is a waterfront road with piers from which yachts and boats offer day trips for fishing and dancing.
